frameworks.name: Features vs. Bugs Framework
frameworks.definition: Every business has permanent structural characteristics (features) that require ongoing management rather than one-time fixes, and temporary fixable problems (bugs); the founder's error is misclassifying features as bugs and breaking working systems to eliminate them.

frameworks.name: Business Scalability Spectrum
frameworks.definition: A three-point spectrum ordering business types by ease-of-start vs. scalability ceiling: service businesses (easy start, hardest to scale quickly) in the middle e-commerce (moderate start cost, moderate scalability), and SaaS/software (hardest to start, easiest to scale at maturity).

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the belief that a business is 'not scalable' is almost always a misdiagnosis: every business category has scaling difficulty, and switching from one service-business type to another will not meaningfully change the growth trajectory because the underlying constraint (human capital) remains the same.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: switching between service categories rather than to SaaS/software
claims.mechanism: Human-capital constraints exist in all service businesses; changing the service vertical replaces one people-management problem with a different but equally constraining people-management problem.
bounded_by: Does not apply to transitions from service to software/SaaS, where the constraint structure genuinely differs

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that 78% of businesses in the United States are service-based businesses, making the desire to escape 'people-based' business constraints statistically irrelevant as an escape hatch for most founders.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: share of US businesses by type

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that service businesses face one of two constraint types: demand-constrained (finding customers is harder than finding workers, e.g., brick-and-mortar fitness) or supply-constrained (finding qualified workers is harder than finding customers, e.g., accounting firms); both types are ultimately solved through promotion, just on opposite sides of the business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: In demand-constrained businesses, promotion targets customers; in supply-constrained businesses, promotion targets potential employees or contractors. The tactic class (promotion/outreach) is identical; only the target differs.
bounded_by: Businesses that alternate between both constraints as they grow

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the painful period between identifying a constraint and the solution taking effect — often three to six months — is the primary moment at which entrepreneurs destructively modify working business models, creating new structural problems on top of the original constraint.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses actively hiring to resolve a supply constraint
claims.mechanism: Founders experience daily pain of an unsolved constraint, which triggers an urge to 'do something'; they change price, deliverable structure, or model rather than tolerating the lag in the already-initiated solution. Changes to a working model introduce new structural problems (e.g., churn rises when service quality falls) without solving the original constraint.

numbers.axis: time from supply-constraint identification to new hire becoming productive

anchors.region: start of promotional cycle (ads, outreach, interviews)

bounded_by: Fast-fix problems that can be resolved within days do not trigger the destructive modification pattern

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that difficulty is a feature, not a bug, of scaling a business: any growing business will continuously encounter slow-fix problems alongside fast-fix problems, and the majority of a founder's career will be spent tolerating painful in-progress solutions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Fast fixes are resolved quickly and leave the system. Slow fixes remain for extended periods, creating persistent operational pain. Once a slow fix completes, a new one always emerges because growth itself generates new constraints.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the actual constraint in most stalled businesses is not the business model or its scalability, but the timeline of founder expectations: the problem is not what the founder wants to achieve, but when they have arbitrarily decided it must happen.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Arbitrary short-timeline demands cause founders to cut corners on hiring, systems, and customer quality, which degrades the business they are trying to grow; extending the timeline to a decade removes the pressure that creates the shortcuts.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses Microsoft and OpenAI as reference points to argue that meaningful global-scale companies require approximately seven to ten years to build from inception to significant scale, and that founders who operate on shorter self-imposed timelines systematically undermine their own growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: companies aiming for global or dominant-market scale

numbers.axis: years from founding to first IPO or major scale milestone

anchors.region: Hormozi's own rule of thumb for most founders

bounded_by: Outlier founders with exceptional resources or market timing may compress timelines

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that every alternative business path carries equally difficult — and likely less familiar — problems, making switching paths economically irrational for experienced founders because the cost of re-learning a new constraint set is additive to the existing problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founders who have been in their industry for one or more years
claims.mechanism: The longer a founder operates in a domain, the more they have mapped its terrain (known failure modes and recovery tactics). Switching domains resets that map to zero, so they face not only the new domain's equally hard problems but also lack the experience to solve them efficiently.
bounded_by: A founder who has accumulated deep skills that transfer directly to the new domain may have lower switching cost

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the compounding benefit of persistence in one business comes from building problem-solving capacity specific to that industry's constraints: the longer a founder has dealt with a specific type of problem, the more effectively they can navigate future iterations of that same problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Repeated exposure to a domain's failure modes creates a mental map of solutions and their timelines; this map is non-transferable and takes years to rebuild in a new domain.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that building a large business — one seeking 30 to 40 years of compounding — requires the founder to say no to effectively all other ideas and opportunities besides the current one, because by pursuing multiple things simultaneously the founder captures none of them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Compounding returns in a single business require sustained input over decades; splitting attention across ideas fragments the compounding and resets the accumulation clock on every new pursuit.

numbers.axis: fraction of own ideas a founder can realistically start

anchors.region: ideas a founder will actually start
ideas worth fully committing to simultaneously

bounded_by: Divisions within a single large operating company — where additional lines extend the core rather than dilute it — may be an exception at sufficient scale

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when founders successfully solve a supply constraint (e.g., hiring enough accountants), they immediately face the inverse demand constraint (too much capacity, needing to fill calendars), leading to margin-degrading behaviors like lowering standards for customer quality; the problem merely shifts polarity rather than disappearing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses that have just resolved a supply constraint by hiring aggressively
claims.mechanism: Excess idle capacity creates payroll pressure; founders lower the bar on customer quality to fill slots, which lowers average contract value and raises churn, while fixed costs (payroll) have already increased — compressing margins from both directions simultaneously.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the desire to eliminate all problems from a business is itself the biggest problem in any business, because it is the proximate cause of founders making changes to working systems, which introduces new problems and the cost of transition on top of the original constraint.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The wish for a problem-free business causes reactive model changes. Each change breaks a working component, generating a new structural problem (pain two), and the act of changing itself incurs a transition cost (pain three). The founder now has three problems instead of one.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Sam Altman's observation — that the idea and initial product are only about 10% of building a business, while execution is 90% — implies founders cannot delegate the execution phase, only the product iteration phase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: share of business-building effort by phase

anchors.region: execution, operations, solving daily and slow-fix problems

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes a brick-and-mortar fitness business as a demand-constrained service: finding willing customers is harder than finding trainers, since fitness enthusiasts and trainers are abundant but people who want to sign up for a service package are scarce.

Alex Hormozi describes an accounting firm as a supply-constrained service: nearly everyone needs accounting done (demand is abundant), but finding competent, high-quality accountants is the binding constraint.

Alex Hormozi walks through the lag timeline of solving a supply constraint: a founder recognizes the need to hire HVAC technicians or accountants, starts ads and outreach, conducts interviews, extends offers, begins training, and only three to six months later does the new hire become productive enough to relieve the constraint — during which the business appears to be standing still despite active effort.

Alex Hormozi describes a founder who is supply-constrained (not enough technicians) and, unable to tolerate the waiting period, changes the deliverable from ten customers per account to twenty — temporarily allowing continued sales but degrading service quality, spiking churn, and introducing a structural margin problem into a business that had previously retained revenue well.

Alex Hormozi uses the 'bricks in a building' analogy: of the infinite possible positions a brick could be placed in the physical world, only one position contributes to holding the building upright. Moving a brick that is already in the right position has a near-zero probability of improving the building's strength and a high probability of weakening it — analogous to changing a business element that is already working.

Alex Hormozi describes the hypothetical resolution of an accounting firm's supply constraint: after building partnerships with accounting schools and creating a recruiting pipeline, the firm now has accountants with empty calendars, excess payroll, and must aggressively acquire customers — lowering quality standards to fill slots, reducing contract value and raising churn while fixed costs have already risen.

Alex Hormozi uses an old-bull/young-bull parable — the young bull wants to run down the hill to procreate with one cow, the old bull says walk slowly and they can have all of them — but then deliberately inverts its business lesson: in entrepreneurship, the inverse is true. A founder who tries to pursue every business opportunity will capture none, whereas sustained focus on one path for decades allows the deepest compounding.

practices.text: When experiencing the painful waiting period of a slow-fix solution, redirect the urge to 'do something' toward accelerating the solution already in progress (e.g., take interviews yourself, speed up the recruiting cycle) rather than modifying the business model.

When evaluating whether to switch to a different business type, enumerate all the problems of the alternative path and honestly assess whether you are better equipped to solve those problems than the ones you currently face.
Operate on a decade-scale time horizon for major business goals; use roughly ten years as the planning unit for building from new idea to significant global scale.

Eliminate FOMO as a performance benchmark: when you can hear about another entrepreneur's success and remain fully committed to your own path without wanting to pivot toward theirs, you have sufficiently developed the focus muscle.
